questions.stem:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.

S1: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

S2: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to S1 and S2 ?
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Both S1 and S2 are false
S1 is true and S2 is false
S1 is false and S2 is true

solutionDiagram.alt: Devices wired in a chain; the CPU sends one INTA signal that passes through them in order.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: An interrupt is a signal from a device asking the CPU to stop and run a small program called the interrupt service routine (ISR). The CPU must learn which device asked, so that it can run that device's ISR. In a vectored interrupt the device itself sends a number (the vector) that points straight to the ISR address. In a non-vectored interrupt there is one common ISR address, so the ISR must first find the source, usually by reading the status of each device in turn. In a daisy chain the devices are wired in a line and the CPU's acknowledge signal travels down the line; the first device that has a request stops the signal and answers. The rule: the work of finding the source is done by software in non-vectored schemes and by hardware in vectored and daisy-chain schemes.

steps.title: Check S1
steps.body: Non-vectored interrupts spend extra time in the ISR polling devices to find the source. Vectored interrupts jump directly. So starting the right ISR takes longer without vectors, and S1 is true.

steps.title: Check S2
steps.body: In a daisy chain the CPU sends one acknowledge signal into the chain and the first requesting device claims it and supplies its identity. The CPU does not poll the devices one by one, so S2 is false. Polling is a different scheme. S1 true and S2 false is option C.

shortcut.body: Spot the word polls in S2: that describes software polling, not the daisy chain, so S2 is false. S1 is the standard textbook comparison, so true. Answer C in under a minute.

traps.text: Treats the daisy chain as polling because the devices are checked in priority order; the check is done by the signal passing along the wires, not by the CPU.
Doubts S1 because both schemes eventually run an ISR; the question is about the time to start it.
Reverses both statements.

recognize.clues: The question names vectored, non-vectored and daisy-chain interrupts and asks how the source device is found, so it is about identifying the interrupting device and the start-up time of its ISR.
recognize.contrast: Software polling reads each status register in turn under CPU control, while a daisy chain finds the source in hardware as the acknowledge signal passes along the line. The word "polls" in S2 describes the first, not the second.

check.body: Test S2 with a chain of four devices where only the third requests. The acknowledge signal passes the first two untouched and the third stops it, so the CPU issued one acknowledge and never read any status register.

sources.label: GATE 2026 CS-2 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: In each scheme, ask who works out which device raised the request: the hardware wiring or a program running on the CPU?
A vectored interrupt hands the CPU the ISR address along with the request. A non-vectored one arrives at a single common entry point with no such address.
For each scheme, decide whether the hardware wiring or software running on the CPU finds the source of the request, and judge each statement against that.
Judge S1 and S2 one at a time as true or false, then look for the option that carries that exact pair.

variation.stem:
Consider two statements about I/O.

S1: In programmed I/O with polling, the CPU reads the status of each device in turn to find one that needs service.

S2: In a vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU must poll the devices after the interrupt to learn which one raised it.

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
S1 is true and S2 is false
S1 is false and S2 is true
Both S1 and S2 are false
variation.explanation: S1 is the definition of polling, so it is true. In a vectored interrupt the device supplies its own vector, so no search by the CPU is needed and S2 is false. The pair "S1 true, S2 false" is the second option.

questions.stem:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

(i) The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. An interrupt is checked only at the end of an instruction, because stopping in the middle would leave the instruction half done and impossible to resume. The rule: finish the instruction, save the PC so the program can resume, then load the PC with the ISR address.

steps.title: Order the steps
steps.body: First (iii): the present instruction completes, so the PC now names the next instruction of the program. Then (i): that PC value is saved. Then (ii): the PC gets the ISR start address, which overwrites the old value, which is why the save must come before it. The order is (iii), (i), (ii): option A.

shortcut.body: Finish, save, jump. Saving must precede the jump or the return address is lost, and the instruction must finish first. Only A fits.

traps.text: Saves the PC before the instruction finishes; the saved value would be the address of an unfinished instruction, or would be stale.
Loads the ISR address before saving, which destroys the return address, and finishes the instruction last.
Jumps to the ISR and then saves the PC, so the saved value is the ISR address.

recognize.clues: The steps are the processor actions on an asynchronous interrupt in a non-pipelined machine: finishing the instruction, saving the program counter and loading the ISR address.
recognize.contrast: An exception raised inside an instruction, such as a page fault, may restart that instruction and so saves a different program counter. An external device interrupt waits for the instruction boundary.

check.body: Return from the ISR by restoring the saved program counter. In the correct order that value is the next instruction of the program, so the program resumes with no instruction repeated or skipped; any other order breaks this.

sources.label: GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: The processor can be stopped at any moment by the device. At what point in an instruction is it safe for the processor to react?
The program counter holds the address of the next instruction to run. An interrupt service routine has its own start address, which also goes into the program counter.
Loading a new value into a register overwrites the old one, so anything that must be kept has to be copied out before the load.
Order the three steps by two constraints: what must already be complete before the program counter value is meaningful, and what must happen before the program counter is overwritten.

variation.stem:
A non-pipelined processor takes an asynchronous device interrupt. The steps below are listed in no particular order.

(i) The ISR ends with a return-from-interrupt instruction that restores the saved program counter.
(ii) The processor saves the program counter.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.
(iv) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
variation.explanation: The instruction finishes first so the program counter names the next instruction. That value is saved before the counter is overwritten with the ISR address. The ISR runs and its last act is the return that restores the saved value, giving (iii), (ii), (iv), (i).

questions.stem: Consider a computer with a 4 MHz processor. Its DMA controller can transfer 8 bytes in 1 cycle from a device to main memory through cycle stealing at regular intervals. Which one of the following is the data transfer rate (in bits per second) of the DMA controller if 1% of the processor cycles are used for DMA?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Direct memory access (DMA) lets a controller move data between a device and memory without the CPU copying each word. In cycle stealing, the DMA controller takes the memory bus for single cycles now and then, so the CPU loses just those cycles. The rate is then (stolen cycles per second) x (bits moved per stolen cycle).

steps.title: Count stolen cycles
steps.body: A 4 MHz processor has 4,000,000 cycles each second. One percent are used for DMA: 40,000 cycles per second.

steps.title: Convert to bits
steps.body: Each stolen cycle moves 8 bytes = 64 bits. Rate = 40,000 x 64 = 2,560,000 bits per second, option C.

shortcut.body: 4,000,000 x 1% = 40,000 cycles; times 64 bits = 2.56 million. Option C by direct product.

traps.text: Drops a factor of 10 by taking 0.1% of the cycles.
Applies the 1% twice (4,000,000 x 0.01 x 0.01 x 8) instead of once.
Takes 0.1% of the cycles (4,000) and multiplies by 8 as if the transfer were 8 bits, which gives 32,000; always convert bytes to bits last.

recognize.clues: The words "cycle stealing", a percentage of processor cycles used for DMA and a word size per cycle tell you to build the rate from stolen cycles times bits per cycle.
recognize.contrast: Burst mode holds the bus for a whole block, so it is described by block length and bus time, not by a percentage of stolen cycles.

check.body: Run the product backwards. Divide 2,560,000 bits per second by 64 bits per cycle to get 40,000 cycles per second, then divide by the 4,000,000 cycles per second available. That recovers exactly 1 percent.

sources.label: GATE 2024 CS2 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: How many processor cycles happen each second, and what fraction of them does the DMA controller take?
In cycle stealing the DMA controller borrows the bus for single cycles, and every borrowed cycle moves a fixed amount of data.
Transfer rate equals stolen cycles per second multiplied by the amount of data moved per stolen cycle. The result must be in bits, so convert bytes at the end.
Find the clock cycles per second from the frequency, take the given percentage of them, then multiply by the bits in one transfer.
The frequency is 4 MHz, which is four million cycles each second. One percent of that is the number of cycles that belong to DMA.

variation.stem: A computer has an 8 MHz processor. Its DMA controller moves 4 bytes in one cycle from a device to main memory by cycle stealing at regular intervals. What is the data transfer rate in bits per second if 2% of the processor cycles are used for DMA?
variation.explanation: There are 8,000,000 cycles per second and 2% of them is 160,000 stolen cycles. Each moves 4 bytes = 32 bits, so the rate is 160,000 x 32 = 51,20,000 bits per second. The other options use bytes instead of bits, 0.2% instead of 2%, or convert bytes to bits twice.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O device and main memory in a stolen cycle
For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the cycle stealing mode
Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU usage than the interrupt driven I/O mechanism
The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: In programmed I/O the CPU sits in a loop reading the device status until it is ready (busy waiting), so it does no other useful work. In interrupt-driven I/O the CPU runs other work and is interrupted only when the device is ready. In DMA the controller moves data itself; cycle stealing takes one bus cycle at a time, and burst mode holds the bus for a whole block. A vectored interrupt supplies the ISR address directly.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: A: in cycle stealing the controller takes one cycle and moves one word. True. B: burst mode keeps the bus and moves many words back to back, avoiding repeated bus arbitration, so higher throughput for bulk data. True. D: a vector gives the ISR address at once, while non-vectored needs a search. True.

steps.title: The false one
steps.body: C claims busy-waiting uses the CPU better than interrupts. It is the opposite: interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU between events. C is false, option C.

shortcut.body: Look for the statement that contradicts the basic fact that polling wastes CPU time. C.

traps.text: Thinks cycle stealing moves a whole block per steal; it moves one word.
Believes cycle stealing is faster because the CPU is less disturbed; that helps the CPU, not the transfer throughput.
Doubts the vector advantage; the vector removes the search for the source.

recognize.clues: The question asks which of four I/O statements is false and mixes CPU usage, DMA modes and interrupt types, so each must be judged by how much CPU time the scheme wastes or how much the bus is held.
recognize.contrast: CPU usage and transfer throughput are different measures: cycle stealing is gentle on the CPU, while burst mode gives the device higher throughput.

check.body: Put numbers on it. If a device takes 1 ms to become ready, a polling CPU spends that whole millisecond looping, while an interrupt-driven CPU spends only the short ISR time and runs other work for the rest. This tells you which scheme uses the CPU better.

sources.label: GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: Only one statement is false. Check each one against what the CPU is actually doing in that scheme.
Ask what the CPU is doing while it waits for a device in programmed I/O, and what it is doing in interrupt-driven I/O.
For each DMA mode, ask how many words move per grant of the bus. For each interrupt type, ask whether the source address arrives with the request.
For each option, decide what the CPU is doing during the wait or during the transfer, and mark the statement that contradicts this.

variation.stem: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: In burst mode DMA, the controller releases the bus after every word so that the CPU can use it
In programmed I/O the CPU is free to run other programs while the device prepares its data
In interrupt-driven I/O, the CPU runs an interrupt service routine for each unit of data the device transfers
In DMA, the CPU copies each word from the device to memory after the controller signals ready
variation.explanation: Burst mode holds the bus for many words, and programmed I/O makes the CPU busy-wait, so the first two are false. In DMA the controller itself moves the data, so the last is false. Interrupt-driven I/O does run an ISR per transfer unit, so the third is true.

questions.stem:
A keyboard connected to a computer is used at a rate of 1 keystroke per second. The computer system polls the keyboard every 10 ms (milli seconds) to check for a keystroke and consumes 100 $\mu$s (micro seconds) for each poll. If it is determined after polling that a key has been pressed, the system consumes an additional 200 $\mu$s to process the keystroke. Let $T_1$ denote the fraction of a second spent in polling and processing a keystroke.

In an alternative implementation, the system uses interrupts instead of polling. An interrupt is raised for every keystroke. It takes a total of 1 ms for servicing an interrupt and processing a keystroke. Let $T_2$ denote the fraction of a second spent in servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke.

The ratio $T_1/T_2$ is ______. (Rounded off to one decimal place)

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Polling means the CPU checks the device at fixed intervals whether or not it has anything to say, so the cost is paid every interval. With interrupts the CPU pays only when an event occurs. For each scheme, time spent per second divided by one second gives the fraction.

steps.title: Polling cost
steps.body: Polls per second = 1 s / 10 ms = 100. Each costs 100 $\mu$s, so 100 x 100 $\mu$s = 10 ms. One keystroke per second adds 200 $\mu$s. $T_1 = 10.2$ ms per second = 0.0102.

steps.title: Interrupt cost and ratio
steps.body: One keystroke per second costs 1 ms, so $T_2 = 0.001$. Ratio = 10.2 / 1 = 10.2.

shortcut.body: Per second: polling 100 x 0.1 ms + 0.2 ms = 10.2 ms; interrupt 1 ms. Ratio 10.2.

traps.text: 10.0 comes from forgetting the 200 microseconds of keystroke processing.
102 comes from mixing milliseconds and microseconds when adding the 200 microseconds.
0.1 results from inverting the ratio.

recognize.clues: Two implementations of the same keyboard are compared by the fraction of each second the CPU spends on I/O: periodic polling versus one interrupt per keystroke.
recognize.contrast: Polling overhead depends on the polling rate and is paid even when idle, while interrupt overhead depends on the event rate. A fast device can flip which one is cheaper.

check.body: Use a bound instead of redoing the sum. Polling alone costs 100 polls x 0.1 ms = 10 ms of every second, against 1 ms for the interrupt, so the ratio must be a little above 10. The keystroke processing adds 0.2 ms to the 10 ms, and 0.2 ms over 1 ms accounts for exactly the 0.2 above 10.

sources.label: GATE 2023 CS answer key, IIT Kanpur (organising institute, PDF author IITK_GATE), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: Work in one second. How many times is the keyboard polled in that second, and how many keystrokes arrive?
Polling pays its cost on every check whether or not a key was pressed. An interrupt scheme pays only when a keystroke actually happens.
Fraction of a second equals time spent in that second divided by one second. Keep every term in the same unit before adding.
Compute T1 as polls per second times the cost of one poll, plus the keystroke processing. Compute T2 from the interrupt time of one keystroke, then divide.
A poll every 10 ms means 100 polls in a second. Convert the 100 microsecond poll cost and the 200 microsecond processing time to the same unit as the 1 ms interrupt time.

variation.stem: A keyboard is used at 1 keystroke per second. The system polls it every 20 ms and spends 50 $\mu$s on each poll. When a poll finds a key pressed, it spends another 300 $\mu$s processing the keystroke. Let $T_1$ be the fraction of a second spent on polling and processing. With interrupts instead, servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke takes 2 ms in total, and $T_2$ is the fraction of a second spent on that. The ratio $T_1/T_2$ is ______. (Rounded off to one decimal place)
variation.explanation: In one second there are 1 s / 20 ms = 50 polls costing 50 x 50 = 2,500 $\mu$s, plus 300 $\mu$s for the keystroke, so $T_1$ = 2,800 $\mu$s per second. The interrupt scheme costs 2,000 $\mu$s, so the ratio is 2,800 / 2,000 = 1.4.

questions.stem: Which one of the following facilitates transfer of bulk data from hard disk to main memory with the highest throughput?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: In the three CPU-driven methods (polling, programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O) every word passes through the CPU, which executes instructions to read the device and write memory. In direct memory access (DMA) a controller sets up the transfer once, then moves the whole block between the disk and memory by itself and interrupts the CPU only at the end. The rule: for bulk data, avoid per-word CPU work.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Polling and programmed I/O waste CPU time waiting and copy word by word. Interrupt-driven I/O pays an interrupt and ISR for each word or small unit. DMA pays one setup and one completion interrupt for the whole block and uses the bus at memory speed. DMA has the highest throughput: option A.

shortcut.body: Bulk data from disk means DMA. No calculation needed.

traps.text: Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU but still moves each word through it and pays an interrupt each time.
Polling and programmed I/O are the same busy-waiting scheme and are the slowest and most CPU-hungry.
Programmed I/O is the same busy-waiting scheme as polling.

recognize.clues: "Bulk data" from a disk to main memory with "highest throughput" points at a block transfer that avoids per-word CPU work.
recognize.contrast: Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU while it waits but still spends an interrupt and a copy on each word, so it suits slow devices with sparse data rather than bulk transfer.

check.body: Take a block of 4,096 words. With interrupt-driven I/O the CPU takes 4,096 interrupts, one per word. With the winning method it handles one set-up and one completion event, so the CPU overhead per word falls by a factor of thousands.

sources.label: GATE 2022 CS answer key, IIT Kharagpur (organising institute, named in the page banner), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: Bulk data means a very large number of words. Which method keeps the CPU out of the per-word work?

Count what the CPU must do for every single word it moves between a disk and memory: instructions to read, instructions to write, and any waiting. Ask which kind of hardware could take that work away.
Throughput for large blocks is highest when per-word overhead is smallest: no busy-waiting, no interrupt per word and no CPU copy.
For each option, list what the CPU does per word and what it does per block, then rank the options by the per-word cost.

variation.stem: A network card must place a large block of received packets into main memory while the CPU keeps executing user programs, with CPU involvement kept to a minimum for the whole block. Which one of the following should be used?
options: Interrupt-driven I/O with one interrupt per packet
DMA with one completion interrupt at the end of the block
Interrupt-driven I/O with one interrupt per word
variation.explanation: The CPU programs the DMA controller once, the controller moves the whole block over the bus on its own, and a single interrupt reports completion. The other methods all make the CPU touch each word, by waiting, copying or servicing an interrupt.

questions.stem: Consider a computer system with DMA support. The DMA module is transferring one 8-bit character in one CPU cycle from a device to memory through cycle stealing at regular intervals. Consider a 2 MHz processor. If 0.5% processor cycles are used for DMA, the data transfer rate of the device is ______ bits per second.

solutionDiagram.alt: A 2 MHz clock with one cycle in every 200 stolen by the DMA controller.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: In cycle stealing the DMA controller takes the bus for single CPU cycles; each stolen cycle moves the data width of one transfer. Rate = stolen cycles per second x bits per stolen cycle.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: A 2 MHz processor has 2,000,000 cycles per second. 0.5% of them is 10,000 cycles per second.

steps.title: Convert
steps.body: Each stolen cycle moves one 8-bit character, so the rate is 10,000 x 8 = 80,000 bits per second.

traps.text: 10,000 results from stopping at cycles per second and reporting characters instead of bits.
640,000 results from treating 8 bytes as moved per cycle (the 2024 Set 2 version used 8 bytes).
800,000 is a slip of 5% for 0.5%.

recognize.clues: "Cycle stealing at regular intervals", a processor frequency, a percentage of cycles used for DMA and a character width together give the rate as stolen cycles times bits per cycle.
recognize.contrast: In burst mode the controller holds the bus for the whole block, so no percentage of stolen cycles is given and the rate is limited by bus speed instead.

check.body: Divide the result back. At 80,000 bits per second and 8 bits per character the device delivers 10,000 characters per second. These need 10,000 stolen cycles, which is 0.5% of 2,000,000 cycles per second, matching the data.

sources.label: GATE 2021 CS-2 answer key, IIT Bombay (organising institute), IIT Guwahati archive copy of the CS-1/CS-2 PDF

hints.text: How many processor cycles occur in one second, and how many of them go to DMA?
In cycle stealing each stolen bus cycle moves one fixed-size unit of data from the device to memory.
Data rate equals stolen cycles per second multiplied by bits moved per stolen cycle. Pay attention to the percentage: 0.5% is five thousandths, not five hundredths.
Convert the clock frequency to cycles per second, take the given percentage, then multiply by the size of one character in bits.
A 2 MHz processor has two million cycles per second. Apply 0.5% to that figure to get the number of stolen cycles.

variation.stem: A computer system has DMA support. The DMA module transfers one 16-bit word in one CPU cycle from a device to memory through cycle stealing at regular intervals. The processor runs at 10 MHz and 0.2% of its cycles are used for DMA. The data transfer rate of the device is ______ bits per second.
variation.explanation: The processor has 10,000,000 cycles per second and 0.2% of them is 20,000 stolen cycles. Each moves 16 bits, so the rate is 20,000 x 16 = 3,20,000 bits per second.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.

I. Daisy chaining is used to assign priorities in attending interrupts.
II. When a device raises a vectored interrupt, the CPU does polling to identify the source of interrupt.
III. In polling, the CPU periodically checks the status bits to know if any device needs its attention.
IV. During DMA, both the CPU and DMA controller can be bus masters at the same time.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A bus master is the unit currently driving the bus; only one unit can drive it at a time. A daisy chain wires devices in a line so that the closest device wins when several request. A vectored interrupt carries the ISR address with it. Polling means the CPU reads device status bits itself.

steps.title: Test each statement
steps.body: I: the position in the chain sets priority, so true. II: a vectored interrupt names its source, so no polling is needed; false. III: that is the definition of polling; true. IV: two masters driving one bus at once would collide, so DMA uses bus arbitration and only one is master at a time; false.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: True: I and III only, option C.

shortcut.body: Cross out II (vectored means no polling) and IV (one master at a time); I and III remain.

traps.text: Accepts II; polling is what vectoring removes.
Accepts IV; the CPU is held off the bus while DMA runs.
Rejects I; daisy chain is the standard hardware priority scheme.

recognize.clues: Four statements mix daisy chaining, vectored interrupts, polling and bus mastership during DMA, so each must be matched with the mechanism it truly describes.
recognize.contrast: Polling is software-driven identification of the source, while vectored interrupts and daisy chains identify it in hardware. Statements swap these roles to create false options.

check.body: Test statement IV by counting drivers. If both CPU and DMA controller were master, both would drive the address lines at once, which is an electrical conflict. Real systems avoid this with bus request and bus grant signals, so the statement fails.

sources.label: GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi (organising institute), print of its paper-and-key web page, IIT Guwahati archive

hints.text: Judge each of the four statements separately as true or false before you look at the options.
Priority, finding the source of a request and checking for readiness are three separate jobs. For each statement, ask which job it talks about and who does it, hardware or a program.
Ask who drives the address lines while a DMA controller is transferring data, and whether the CPU could drive the same lines in that moment.
Decide each statement, write down the set of true ones, and then find the option that lists exactly that set.

variation.stem:
Consider the following statements.

I. In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the interrupt service routine must determine which device raised the interrupt.
II. In a daisy chain, a device nearer to the CPU gets higher priority than a device farther away.
III. During burst mode DMA, the CPU can use the bus at any time.
IV. In programmed I/O, the CPU waits in a loop until the device is ready.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
variation.explanation: I is true because a single common entry point forces software to find the source. II is the usual daisy chain rule. III is false because burst mode holds the bus until the block is done. IV is the definition of busy-waiting. The true set is I, II and IV.

questions.stem:
The following are some events that occur after a device controller issues an interrupt while process L is under execution.

(P) The processor pushes the process status of L onto the control stack.
(Q) The processor finishes the execution of the current instruction.
(R) The processor executes the interrupt service routine.
(S) The processor pops the process status of L from the control stack.
(T) The processor loads the new PC value based on the interrupt.

Which one of the following is the correct order in which the events above occur?

solutionDiagram.alt: The five events in order along a timeline.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: An interrupt is acted on only after the current instruction ends. The CPU then saves the state of the running process (its status and PC) on the control stack so it can resume later, switches the PC to the ISR address, runs the ISR, and finally restores the saved state.

steps.title: Order
steps.body: Q: finish the instruction. P: push the status of L. T: load the new PC for the interrupt. R: run the ISR. S: pop the status of L to resume. The order is QPTRS: option A.

shortcut.body: Finish, push, load PC, run, pop. Pop is always last and Q first, which leaves only A.

traps.text: Pushes first and finishes the current instruction last (Q at the end), so the interrupt is taken mid-instruction.
Loads the PC before saving, so the old state is lost, and pops after Q.
Loads the new PC before pushing the status, so the return state is overwritten.

recognize.clues: The question lists the steps after a device controller raises an interrupt and asks for their order, so it is the standard interrupt-service sequence: finish, save, redirect, run, restore.
recognize.contrast: Programmed I/O has the CPU test the device itself and never saves a process status to a control stack. Here the device initiates the transfer of control, which is what forces the save and restore.

check.body: Swap any adjacent pair in QPTRS and see what breaks. Putting T before P overwrites the PC of L before it is saved, so the return address is lost. Putting S before R pops the state before the handler has run. Putting Q after P means the interrupt cuts an instruction in half. Only the given order survives all three swaps.

sources.label: GATE 2018 CS final answer key (organised by IIT Guwahati), gateexam.info copy

hints.text: Which event must come first so that the CPU never leaves an instruction half done, and which must come last so that L can carry on?
An interrupt is a request that the CPU notices only at a safe point. Afterwards it must be able to return to exactly where L stopped.
State that is still needed for the return must be stored before anything overwrites it, and it is only taken back after the handler has finished.
Notice that the events are not listed in time order in the question. Fix the two ends of the sequence first, then decide the order of the pair whose positions depend on what must be kept safe.

variation.stem:
A device raises an interrupt request while process L is in the middle of executing an instruction. The events below occur in some order.

(P) The processor saves the PC and status of L.
(Q) The device raises the interrupt request.
(R) The processor executes the interrupt service routine.
(S) The processor resumes L from the saved state.
(T) The processor finishes the instruction it was executing.

Which one of the following is the correct order of these events?
variation.explanation: The request (Q) comes first, and the current instruction is then completed (T). Only after that is the state of L saved (P), the handler run (R) and L resumed (S). That is QTPRS, the last option.
